summary: This informational document gives a framework for supporting multicast traffic in networks that use Network Virtualization over Layer 3. It covers both infrastructure multicast and application-specific multicast, and the mechanisms and control and data plane options for delivering them.

plainLanguage.summary: In virtual networks that run on top of a real one, group messages have to reach many places. This lays out the ways to do that.

questions: how does multicast work in nvo3
subtitle: How to handle group messages in virtual networks

tldr.problem: Network virtualization over Layer 3 (NVO3) runs virtual networks on top of physical networks, but multicast (sending to a group) is hard to support because virtual machines live on different physical servers that only understand unicast (point-to-point) communication.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC frameworks four main approaches: no multicast support (for applications that don't need it), replicating packets at the source, using a central multicast service node, or leveraging IP multicast in the physical network.
tldr.outcome: Network designers can choose the multicast strategy that fits their needs: cost-effective, simple, or optimal depending on how many groups and servers they have.

today: RFC 8293 is an Informational document providing guidance for NVO3 implementations. It remains current and is actively used by data center architects choosing multicast strategies for virtual network deployments.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Network Virtualization over Layer 3 (NVO3) is a technology used to build large data centers where many customers' networks run on top of the same physical infrastructure. It is essential for virtualized servers that host multiple virtual machines (VMs).

The RFC distinguishes two types of multicast. Infrastructure multicast refers to network services that require broadcast or multicast delivery, such as ARP (address resolution), DHCP (network configuration), and multicast DNS. Application-specific multicast is traffic generated by user applications, such as video streaming or collaborative software, that needs to reach multiple recipients.
sections.plainLanguage: Virtual networks run on top of real networks. They need to send messages to groups of machines. This document explains the ways to do that.

sections.title: Four Multicast Mechanisms
sections.content: The document presents four main approaches. No multicast support works only when all application traffic is unicast and only infrastructure multicast (like ARP) requires broadcast. Replication at the source has the originating virtual edge (NVE) send copies of each multicast packet to every relevant destination, but this consumes a lot of bandwidth and CPU. Replication at a multicast service node sends multicast packets to a central point which replicates them, reducing load on source edges but creating a single point of failure and potential latency issues. Finally, IP multicast in the underlay leverages native multicast support in the physical network itself, avoiding most replication overhead but requiring that the physical infrastructure supports multicast protocols.
sections.plainLanguage: Option one: don't support group messages at all. Option two: the sender copies the message to everyone. Option three: send it to a helper that copies it. Option four: use the real network's group message feature.

sections.title: Source NVE Replication
sections.content:
In this approach, an NVE maintains a list of all other NVEs that contain receivers interested in a particular multicast group. When it sends a multicast packet, it replicates the packet and sends one copy to each relevant NVE. To track receiver interest, NVEs perform IGMP/MLD snooping (listening to membership reports) and may coordinate with a Network Virtualization Authority (NVA) that maintains global membership information.

The main advantage is that no support is needed from the physical network—only unicast is required. However, the drawbacks are significant. For a subnet spread across 50 physical servers, every multicast packet must be replicated 50 times at the source NVE, consuming network bandwidth and NVE CPU. Additionally, when a virtual machine moves between servers, the replication list must be updated, which becomes complex in dynamic environments.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender copies the message and sends one to each destination that needs it. Simple but wasteful when many places need the same message.

sections.title: Multicast Service Node Replication
sections.content:
This approach designates a special Multicast Service Node (MSN) to handle multicast replication. All multicast packets are sent to the MSN using a unicast tunnel, and the MSN creates multiple copies and sends them onward to destination NVEs. The MSN learns which receivers are interested in each group by querying NVEs with IGMP/MLD messages or by receiving snooped membership information from NVEs.

The benefit is reduced load on individual NVEs—they no longer replicate packets locally. However, the MSN becomes a bottleneck and single point of failure. If the MSN is unavailable, multicast stops working. Additionally, links between the MSN and edge nodes still carry multiple copies of the same traffic, and there may be suboptimal paths. Path preservation is also an issue: if an MSN creates copies, the original source IP address must be maintained in the copies for data-plane learning to work correctly.
sections.plainLanguage: Send the message to a special device that copies it to everyone. Less work for senders, but the special device becomes a bottleneck.

sections.title: IP Multicast in the Underlay
sections.content:
When the physical network supports IP multicast (via PIM or similar protocols), NVEs can use underlay multicast instead of application-layer replication. An NVE encapsulates virtual multicast traffic with a multicast address in the physical network's header and sends it over native multicast. The physical network's routers handle replication, avoiding both source-node and centralized-node bottlenecks.

The advantage is optimal efficiency and scalability. However, this approach requires the physical network to support multicast, which not all networks do. Additionally, there are challenges in mapping virtual multicast groups to physical ones, as the lower 23 bits of IP addresses map to MAC addresses and Layer 2 pruning can cause unexpected aliasing. Provisioning addresses for each group also becomes a management concern. With BIDIR-PIM, the number of flows required scales linearly with multicast groups (not also sources), though many vendors still lack full BIDIR-PIM support.
sections.plainLanguage: Use the real network's built-in group messaging. Most efficient but only works if the physical network speaks multicast.

sections.title: Deployment Considerations
sections.content:
In practice, implementations often use more than one of these mechanisms simultaneously. For instance, Option 1 (no multicast) might be used for minimizing ARP/ND broadcast, while application-specific multicast uses Option 2 or 3. For small multicast groups, source or service-node replication works well, while for large groups, underlay multicast becomes preferable.

Additional challenges include handling multicast-agnostic NVEs (hypervisor-based edges that do not recognize IGMP/MLD frames) and managing dynamic VM placement. When VMs are added, deleted, or moved between servers, membership information must be updated quickly to prevent traffic from reaching outdated locations. The RFC notes that emerging technologies like Bit Indexed Explicit Replication (BIER) may provide future optimizations.
sections.plainLanguage: Real networks mix and match these approaches. Small groups might use one method, large ones another. And when virtual machines move, you have to update where the messages should go.
